Conversations.Prompt: I need a bash script that executes `feh` pointing at a particular folder. It should display each of the images in the folder chronologically by capture date. The script should also repeat once it finishes all of the pictures. It needs to be able to acquire new pictures as they are added to the folder and to stop displaying images once they are removed. Ideally the script does a simple dissolve between images and a simple zoom on the image, but these are not necessary requirements.
Conversations.Answer: Here's a basic bash script that uses feh to display images from a specific directory. In this script, I'm using the -r option to recursively look into the directory, -S option to sort the images by file modification time, and -D option to set the delay between slides. Please replace /path/to/your/directory with the actual path to your directory:[CODE_BLOCK_0]This script will run in an infinite loop, loading new images and removing old ones each time feh is called.Unfortunately, feh does not natively support transition effects such as dissolve or zoom between images. For that, you might need a more advanced slideshow software. There are other tools like imagemagick that can do these effects, but they cannot be incorporated into a real-time slideshow as easily.Please note that this script assumes that the images are being saved with their capture time as the file's modification time. If your camera is saving the capture time in the file's EXIF data, then you would need to use a tool like jhead to adjust the file's modification time to match the capture time before running the script.

ListOfCode.Content:
#!/bin/bash
while true
do
    feh -r -S mtime -D 5 /path/to/your/directory
    sleep 1
done

Conversations.Prompt: Give me the jhead script and add functionality that given a list of image tags, I want to only display images matching at least one of the allowlisted tags.
Conversations.Answer: Here's a more advanced script using jhead to set the file's modification time to the image's capture time, and using exiftool to filter images based on a list of tags.Please install jhead and exiftool if you haven't already. You can install these tools using the following commands in a Debian-based system:[CODE_BLOCK_0]Here's the script:[CODE_BLOCK_1]Please replace /path/to/your/directory with the path to your images and replace tag1, tag2, tag3 with the tags you want to allow. This script will make a temporary copy of the images that match the tags, and then display those images.Remember, this script will not update the slideshow in real-time when new images are added or when tags are changed. If you need this functionality, you might want to consider running the script at regular intervals using a tool like cron.Finally, this script assumes that the tags you're looking for are stored in the 'Keywords' EXIF field. If they're stored in a different field, you'll need to adjust the exiftool command accordingly.

ListOfCode.Content:
sudo apt-get install jhead
sudo apt-get install libimage-exiftool-perl

#!/bin/bash

# Folder containing images
dir="/path/to/your/directory"

# Allowed tags
allowed_tags=("tag1" "tag2" "tag3")

# Set the modification time to the capture time
for img in "$dir"/*
do
    jhead -ft "$img"
done

# Create a temporary directory to store images with allowed tags
temp_dir=$(mktemp -d)

for tag in "${allowed_tags[@]}"
do
    for img in $(exiftool -q -r -if '$Keywords =~ /'"$tag"'/i' -p '$Directory/$FileName' "$dir")
    do
        cp "$img" "$temp_dir"
    done
done

# Display images from the temporary directory
while true
do
    feh -r -S mtime -D 5 "$temp_dir"
    sleep 1
done

Conversations.Prompt: Can I get a performance improvement by linking instead of copying the images?
Conversations.Answer: Yes, creating symbolic links (also known as "symlinks") instead of copying files can improve performance and save disk space. Copying files is a relatively slow operation that involves reading the entire contents of the original file and writing it to a new location. By contrast, creating a symbolic link is a quick operation that simply creates a new directory entry pointing to the existing file. This operation is nearly instantaneous, regardless of the size of the original file.In the context of your script, using symbolic links means that the slideshow will display faster when it's initially started, especially if there are many large images to display.Here's how you can modify the script to use symbolic links:[CODE_BLOCK_0]This script works the same as the previous one, but it creates symbolic links in the temporary directory instead of copying the images. The ln -s command is used to create the symbolic links.Remember to replace /path/to/your/directory with the path to your images and replace tag1, tag2, tag3 with the tags you want to allow.

# Folder containing images
dir="/path/to/your/directory"

# Allowed tags

Conversations.Prompt: Does feh interpret symbolic links properly?
Conversations.Answer: Yes, feh can handle symbolic links correctly. When it encounters a symbolic link, it will follow the link and display the image file that the link points to.This makes symbolic links a good way to create a temporary "playlist" of images for feh to display, without needing to move or copy the actual image files. This is especially useful in your case, where you want to filter the images based on metadata tags.So, using symbolic links in the script as suggested in the previous message should work correctly with feh. Conversations.Prompt: Finally, I periodically change the images in my folder and the set of allowed tags every 24 hours using a cron job on a separate script. I want this script to load the new tags and display the new images
Conversations.Answer: If your images and allowed tags are updated every 24 hours and you want to reflect these changes in your slideshow, you can modify the script to run in a daily loop.However, because you're dealing with a temporary directory, you'll need to clean up the old symbolic links before creating new ones. Here's how you can modify the script:[CODE_BLOCK_0]In this script, I have added a few things:A cleanup command (rm -f "$temp_dir"/*) at the start of the loop to remove the old symbolic links.A command (mapfile -t allowed_tags < /path/to/your/tags/file) to load the new allowed tags from a file. Replace /path/to/your/tags/file with the path to your file containing the allowed tags. This file should have one tag per line.A sleep command (sleep 86400) to wait for 24 hours before the next iteration of the loop.With these modifications, your script will reflect changes to your images and allowed tags every 24 hours.

#!/bin/bash

# Folder containing images
dir="/path/to/your/directory"

# Create a temporary directory to store links to images with allowed tags
temp_dir=$(mktemp -d -p /tmp image_links.XXXXXX)

while true
do
    # Clean up the old links
    rm -f "$temp_dir"/*

    # Load the new allowed tags from a file
    mapfile -t allowed_tags < /path/to/your/tags/file

    # Set the modification time to the capture time
    for img in "$dir"/*
    do
        jhead -ft "$img"
    done

    for tag in "${allowed_tags[@]}"
    do
        for img in $(exiftool -q -r -if '$Keywords =~ /'"$tag"'/i' -p '$Directory/$FileName' "$dir")
        do
            ln -s "$img" "$temp_dir"
        done
    done

    # Display images from the temporary directory
    feh -r -S mtime -D 5 "$temp_dir"
    sleep 1

    # Wait for 24 hours before the next iteration
    sleep 86400
done

Conversations.Prompt: I want to use sed in a script to replace the substring '/path/to/your/slideshow_script.sh' within its line. It is in the file called slideshow.service in the same directory as my setup.sh script. I intend to replace the path with the actual path to this file on this, which I know because I have programmatically fetched the current directory of where the script is executing from.
Conversations.Answer: Assuming you have the current directory stored in a variable, you can use sed to replace the placeholder path with the actual path in your slideshow.service file. Here's how you can do it:[CODE_BLOCK_0]In this script, $(pwd) is used to get the current directory, and sed -i is used to modify the slideshow.service file in-place. The s|old|new|g command replaces all occurrences of old with new.Please note that I'm using the pipe character (|) as the delimiter in the sed command instead of the usual slash (/). This is because the replacement string contains slashes, and using a slash as the delimiter would confuse sed. You can use any character as the delimiter in a sed command, and it's common to use a character other than slash when the strings you're dealing with contain slashes.

ListOfCode.Content:
#!/bin/bash

# Store the current directory in a variable
current_dir=$(pwd)

# Use sed to replace the placeholder path in the slideshow.service file
sed -i "s|/path/to/your/slideshow_script.sh|$current_dir/slideshow_script.sh|g" slideshow.service

Conversations.Prompt: If I source a file that doesn't exist, is this an error?
Conversations.Answer: Yes, if you try to source a file that doesn't exist in a bash script, it will result in an error message, and the exit status of the source command will be non-zero.Here's an example:[CODE_BLOCK_0]When you run this, it will print an error message like:[CODE_BLOCK_1]And the echo $? command will print 1, indicating that the previous command (source) exited with an error.However, this error won't automatically terminate the script unless you've set the -e (or set -e) option, which causes the shell to exit if any invoked command exits with a non-zero status.

echo $?
bash: /path/to/nonexistent/file: No such file or directory

Conversations.Prompt: If I want to not automatically exit, can I use the `|| true` pattern?
Conversations.Answer: Yes, you can use the || true pattern to prevent your script from exiting if a particular command fails. When used in a command pipeline, the || operator will only execute the command to its right if the command to its left exits with a non-zero status (indicating failure).So if you write source /path/to/nonexistent/file || true, the source command will fail, but then the true command will run and exit with a zero status, effectively "ignoring" the failure of the source command.Here's how you can use it:[CODE_BLOCK_0]Even if the file doesn't exist and the source command fails, the script won't exit and will continue to run the remaining commands.This is a common pattern used in shell scripts when you want to try running a command that might fail, and you want the script to continue running regardless. However, be aware that this means any errors or problems with the source command will be silently ignored, which might not be what you want if the success of the source command is important to the rest of your script.

Conversations.Prompt: Should I ever source a script to execute it from within another script as opposed to just using ./script.sh?
Conversations.Answer: Whether you should source a script (source script.sh or . script.sh) or execute it (./script.sh) depends on what you want to achieve.Sourcing a script (source script.sh or . script.sh): This reads and executes commands from the filename argument in the current shell context. If the script sets environmental variables or changes the current directory, these changes will be reflected in the shell that sourced the script. This is often used for loading environment variables or shell configuration from a script.Executing a script (./script.sh): This runs the script in a new shell process. Any environmental variables set or directory changes made in the script will not affect the calling shell. This is the usual way to run scripts that perform a series of commands and don't need to modify the environment of the calling shell.So, if you want the script to modify the environment of the calling script (for example, setting environment variables), use source. If you want the script to perform actions (like processing data) and its environment changes shouldn't affect the calling script, use ./.Remember that scripts need to have execute permissions (chmod +x script.sh) to be run with ./. Sourcing a script with source or . doesn't require execute permissions, as it's read and executed by the current shell.

Conversations.Prompt: What then is the purpose of the export keyword?
Conversations.Answer: The export keyword in a shell script or terminal session is used to make a variable available to subprocesses of the shell where the export command is run. This means that the exported variable can be accessed by any scripts or programs that are run from the same shell after the variable is exported.For example, if you run the following commands in a shell:[CODE_BLOCK_0]Then script.sh will be able to access the value of VAR:[CODE_BLOCK_1]This script would print "Hello, world!".However, export does not make the variable permanently available in different terminal sessions or in parent processes. It also does not make the variable available to scripts that are run in their own shell (i.e., scripts that are not sourced).In the context of your previous question, sourcing a script allows all variables (not just those marked with export) to be used in the calling script. But those variables will not be available to other scripts that the calling script runs, unless those scripts are also sourced. To make variables available to scripts that are run (not sourced) from the calling script, you would need to export those variables.

#!/bin/bash
set -e

echo "Starting the image download script..."
echo "Downloading images from SmugMug by album id..."

echo "Getting the directory of the script..."
SCRIPT_DIR=$( cd -- "$( dirname -- "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}" )" &> /dev/null && pwd )

pushd "${SCRIPT_DIR}"

echo "Getting album id..."
source get-album-names.sh

echo "Loading environment variables..."
set -o allexport
source .env || true
source .config
set +o allexport

ALBUM_DIR="${SCRIPT_DIR}/images/${ALBUM_NAME}"
echo "Creating album directory at: ${ALBUM_DIR}"
mkdir -p "${ALBUM_DIR}"
pushd "${ALBUM_DIR}"

echo "Getting API key and secret from environment variables..."
API_KEY=${SMUGMUG_API_KEY}
API_SECRET=${SMUGMUG_API_SECRET}

echo "Constructing URL..."
URL="https://api.smugmug.com/api/v2/album/${ALBUM_ID}!images?APIKey=${API_KEY}"

echo "Making request to SmugMug API..."
response=$(curl -s -H "Accept: application/json" -H "Authorization: Basic $(echo -n "${API_KEY}:${API_SECRET}" | base64 --wrap=0)" -X GET ${URL})

echo "Parsing the response..."
mapfile -t image_data < <(echo $response | jq -r '.Response.AlbumImage[] | "\(.FileName)=\(.ArchivedUri)"')

echo "Downloading new images and removing old images..."
declare -A present_images

for i in "${image_data[@]}"
do
    local IMAGE_NAME="$(echo "${i%%=*}" | sed 's/[\\/:*?"<>|]/-/g')"
    local IMAGE_URI="${i#*=}"
    present_images["${IMAGE_NAME}"]=1

    if [[ ! -f "${IMAGE_NAME}" ]]; then
        echo "Downloading ${IMAGE_NAME} from ${IMAGE_URI}..."
        curl -o "${IMAGE_NAME}" $IMAGE_URI
    fi

    jhead -ft "${IMAGE_NAME}"
done

for file in *
do
    if [[ -f "$file" ]] && [[ -z ${present_images["$file"]} ]]; then
        echo "Deleting old image: $file"
        rm "$file"
    fi
done

IMAGES_DIR="${SCRIPT_DIR}/images/feh"
echo "Removing old symbolic links in: ${IMAGES_DIR}"
rm -f "${IMAGES_DIR}/*"

echo "Splitting ALLOWED_KEYWORDS into an array..."
allowed_keywords=($(IFS=":"; echo $ALLOWED_KEYWORDS))

echo "Creating symbolic links for images that match allowed keywords..."
for keyword in "${allowed_keywords[@]}"
do
    for img in $(exiftool -q -r -if '$Keywords =~ /'"$keyword"'/i' -p '$Directory/$FileName' "$ALBUM_DIR")
    do
        ln -s "$img" "$IMAGES_DIR"
    done
done

popd
popd

echo "Image download and clean-up completed."

# Github PR Fetch Extension for Firefox

This is a simple Firefox extension that adds a 'git fetch' command to GitHub pull request pages, making it easy to fetch and check out pull requests locally.

## How to use

1. Clone this repository: `git clone https://github.com/<YourUsername>/Github_PR_Fetch_Extension.git`

2. Open Firefox, and enter `about:debugging` in the URL bar.

3. Click "This Firefox" (in newer versions of Firefox) or "Load Temporary Add-on" (in older versions).

4. Open the `Github_PR_Fetch_Extension` directory and select any file inside the directory.

The extension should now be temporarily installed, and you'll see it listed in your add-ons.

When you visit a pull request page on GitHub, e.g., `https://github.com/<user>/<repo>/pull/<number>`, you will find the git fetch command just below the discussion header. A copy button is provided for convenience.

## Uninstall

If you want to uninstall the extension, go to `about:debugging`, click on "This Firefox", find the extension in the list, and click "Remove".

## Support

Please [open an issue](https://github.com/<YourUsername>/Github_PR_Fetch_Extension/issues/new) for support.

Conversations.Answer: In JavaScript, there is no insertAfter method on DOM elements. insertBefore is used to insert nodes at any position in the child node list.To make an insertAfter, you would use insertBefore and specify the next sibling of the element as the reference node, which makes it equivalent to an insertAfter.But, because you want to insert the fetchDiv after header and not before its next sibling, you would actually want the insertBefore to reference the nextSibling of header's nextSibling.But you should handle the case where header.nextSibling might be null (which means header is the last child). Thankfully, if the second parameter of insertBefore is null, it behaves just like appendChild:[CODE_BLOCK_0]This code will insert fetchDiv right after header even if header is the last child. If header.nextSibling is null, header.nextSibling.nextSibling will be undefined, so it falls back to null and insertBefore behaves like appendChild.

Conversations.Prompt:
modifiziere 

rsync_command = [
            "rsync", "-abP", "--delete", "--delete-excluded",
            "--link-dest=" + previous_version_path,
            source_path, current_version_path
        ]

so, dass folgender fehler nichtmehr auftritt:

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/usr/local/sbin/backup-to-usb.python", line 62, in <module>
    main()
  File "/usr/local/sbin/backup-to-usb.python", line 44, in main
    "--link-dest=" + previous_version_path,
    ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "NoneType") to str
Conversations.Answer: Dieser Fehler wird durch den Versuch verursacht, None zu einer Zeichenkette zu addieren. In Python ergibt dies einen TypeError. Es scheint, dass previous_version_path manchmal None ist. Sie können diesen Fehler beheben, indem Sie überprüfen, ob previous_version_path None ist, bevor Sie es zur Zeichenkette hinzufügen. Wenn es None ist, sollten Sie den Parameter --link-dest nicht in das rsync-Kommando einfügen. Hier ist, wie Sie Ihren Code ändern könnten:[CODE_BLOCK_0]In diesem modifizierten Code wird previous_version_path nur dann zu rsync_command hinzugefügt, wenn es nicht None ist. Das extend-Methode wird dann verwendet, um source_path und current_version_path zur Liste hinzuzufügen, unabhängig davon, ob previous_version_path None ist oder nicht.

Conversations.Prompt: was ist in diesem fall der unterschied zwischen extend and append
Conversations.Answer: Die append() und extend() Methoden in Python haben ähnliche Funktionen, aber sie werden in unterschiedlichen Kontexten verwendet.append(): Fügt das gesamte Objekt am Ende der Liste hinzu.[CODE_BLOCK_0]In diesem Beispiel wird die Liste [4, 5] als einzelnes Element an das Ende von my_list angehängt, wodurch eine verschachtelte Liste entsteht.extend(): Fügt die Elemente des iterierbaren Objekts am Ende der Liste hinzu.[CODE_BLOCK_1]In diesem Beispiel werden die Elemente der Liste [4, 5] an das Ende von my_list angehängt, wodurch die ursprüngliche Liste erweitert wird.In Ihrem speziellen Fall, wenn Sie die append() Methode anstelle von extend() verwenden, um source_path und current_version_path hinzuzufügen, würde dies dazu führen, dass eine verschachtelte Liste erstellt wird, was nicht das gewünschte Verhalten ist. Daher ist es besser, extend() zu verwenden, um diese Elemente zur Liste rsync_command hinzuzufügen.

ListOfCode.Content:
my_list = [1, 2, 3]
my_list.append([4, 5])
print(my_list)  # Ausgabe: [1, 2, 3, [4, 5]]

my_list = [1, 2, 3]
my_list.extend([4, 5])
print(my_list)  # Ausgabe: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

Conversations.Prompt:
Optimize the following script:

#!/bin/bash
# @param $1 hostname from which backup should be pulled

echo "pulling backups from: $1" &&

# error counter
errors=0 &&

echo "loading meta data..." &&

remote_host="backup@$1" &&
echo "host address:         $remote_host" &&

remote_machine_id="$( (ssh "$remote_host" sha256sum /etc/machine-id) | head -c 64 )" &&
echo "remote machine id:    $remote_machine_id" &&

general_backup_machine_dir="/Backups/$remote_machine_id/" &&
echo "backup dir:           $general_backup_machine_dir" &&

remote_backup_types="$(ssh "$remote_host" "find $general_backup_machine_dir -maxdepth 1 -type d -execdir basename {} ;")" &&
echo "backup types:          $remote_backup_types" || exit 1

for backup_type in $remote_backup_types; do
  if [ "$backup_type" != "$remote_machine_id" ]; then
    echo "backup type:              $backup_type" &&
    
    general_backup_type_dir="$general_backup_machine_dir""$backup_type/" &&
    general_versions_dir="$general_backup_type_dir" &&
    local_previous_version_dir="$(ls -d $general_versions_dir* | tail -1)" &&
    echo "last local backup:      $local_previous_version_dir" &&

    remote_backup_versions="$(ssh "$remote_host" ls -d "$general_backup_type_dir"\*)" &&
    echo "remote backup versions:   $remote_backup_versions" &&


    remote_last_backup_dir=$(echo "$remote_backup_versions" | tail -1) &&
    echo "last remote backup:       $remote_last_backup_dir" &&

    remote_source_path="$remote_host:$remote_last_backup_dir/" &&
    echo "source path:              $remote_source_path" &&

    local_backup_destination_path=$remote_last_backup_dir &&
    echo "backup destination:       $local_backup_destination_path" &&

    echo "creating local backup destination folder..." &&
    mkdir -vp "$local_backup_destination_path" &&

    echo "starting backup..." &&
    rsync_command='rsync -abP --delete --delete-excluded --rsync-path="sudo rsync" --link-dest="'$local_previous_version_dir'" "'$remote_source_path'" "'$local_backup_destination_path'"' &&
    echo "executing:                $rsync_command" &&
    eval "$rsync_command" || ((errors+=1));
  fi
done
exit $errors;

#!/bin/bash

import pandas as pd

import openpyxl

# Change to the directory containing your excel files

        # Load the workbook
        workbook = openpyxl.load_workbook(file)

The source is in a private GitHub repo, and after Netlify successfully builds and deploys the latest version, a GitHub Actions workflow is triggered which builds a PDF version of the home page and stores it as a versioned GitHub release artifact.

I'd like to automatically make the latest version of that PDF available on my website by visiting the URL https://www.scottatron.com/CV.pdf

The resulting PDF download should use the original versioned filename so that people are clear which version they're looking at if they download it.

Could you please suggest how I can achieve this using Netlify and GitHub?
Conversations.Answer: Sure, you can achieve this by using a combination of GitHub Actions, Netlify Functions, and Netlify Redirects. Here's a step-by-step guide:GitHub Actions: First, you need to create a GitHub Action that triggers when a new release is created. This action should get the URL of the latest PDF artifact and store it somewhere accessible. A good option would be to store it as a JSON file in your repository.Here's an example of what this GitHub Action might look like:[CODE_BLOCK_0]This action will create a pdf-url.json file in the public directory of your repository with the URL of the latest PDF.Netlify Functions: Next, you need to create a Netlify Function that will redirect to the URL stored in the pdf-url.json file. This function will be triggered when someone visits https://www.scottatron.com/CV.pdf.Here's an example of what this function might look like:[CODE_BLOCK_1]This function should be placed in your functions directory (e.g., ./netlify/functions/redirect.js).Netlify Redirects: Finally, you need to set up a redirect in your netlify.toml file to redirect https://www.scottatron.com/CV.pdf to your Netlify Function.Here's an example of what this might look like:[CODE_BLOCK_2]This will ensure that when someone visits https://www.scottatron.com/CV.pdf, they will be redirected to the latest PDF.Please note that this is a high-level overview and you might need to adjust the code to fit your specific needs. Also, make sure to test everything in a safe environment before deploying it to production.

ListOfCode.Content:
name: Update Latest PDF URL

on:
  release:
    types: [published]

jobs:
  update_url:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v2

      - name: Get latest release info
        id: get_info
        uses: actions/github-script@v5
        with:
          script: |
            const { data: { assets } } = await github.rest.repos.getReleaseByTag({
              owner: context.repo.owner,
              repo: context.repo.repo,
              tag: context.ref.replace('refs/tags/', '')
            });
            const pdfAsset = assets.find(asset => asset.name.endsWith('.pdf'));
            return pdfAsset.browser_download_url;

      - name: Update PDF URL
        run: echo '{ "url": "${{ steps.get_info.outputs.result }}" }' > ./public/pdf-url.json
        shell: bash

      - name: Commit and push
        run: |
          git config --local user.email "action@github.com"
          git config --local user.name "GitHub Action"
          git add ./public/pdf-url.json
          git commit -m "Update PDF URL" && git push

[[redirects]]
  from = "/CV.pdf"
  to = "/.netlify/functions/redirect"
  status = 302

import { readAttention } from "../attention/readAttention.js"
import yaml from 'js-yaml';
import { getSystemPromptIfNeeded } from './getSystemPromptIfNeeded.js';
import { resolveTemplateVariables } from './resolveTemplateVariables.js';
import { extractTemplateVars } from './extractTemplateVars.js';
import { loadPromptDescriptor } from './loadPromptDescriptor.js';
import { loadTaskTemplate } from './loadTaskTemplate.js';
import { loadFormatTemplate } from './loadFormatTemplate.js';
import loadDefaults from './promptDescriptorDefaults.js';

const createPrompt = async (userInput) => {
  let promptDescriptorDefaults = await loadDefaults();
  let promptDescriptor = yaml.load(await loadPromptDescriptor());

  // Fill in the defaults from promptDescriptorDefaults.js
  promptDescriptor = { ...promptDescriptorDefaults, ...promptDescriptor };

  let templateVars = extractTemplateVars(promptDescriptor);
  templateVars = await resolveTemplateVariables(templateVars);

  const attention = await readAttention(promptDescriptor.attention);
  const task = await loadTaskTemplate(promptDescriptor.task, templateVars);

  const format = await loadFormatTemplate(promptDescriptor.format, templateVars);
  const system = await getSystemPromptIfNeeded();
  const saveto = promptDescriptor.saveto;
  return {
    prompt: `${system}# Working set\n\n${attention.join("\n")}\n\n# Task\n\n${task}\n\n# Output Format\n\n${format}\n\n${userInput ? userInput : ""}`,
    saveto
  };
}

export { createPrompt };

Conversations.Prompt: How does markdownIt works? Why did you choose it over the default, and why over others?
Conversations.Answer: markdown-it is a very powerful and flexible markdown parser and renderer for Node.js. It's highly extensible and customizable with plugins, and it supports all markdown syntax features, including some features not found in other markdown parsers.Here's a brief explanation of how markdown-it works in the context of the script provided:markdownIt() initializes a new markdown-it instance with certain options. html: true enables HTML tags in the source, linkify: true autoconverts URL-like text to links, and typographer: true enables some language-neutral replacement and typographic symbols.highlight is a function that gets called whenever markdown-it encounters code blocks in the markdown source. Here it's using highlight.js to highlight the code in the code blocks. If a language is specified with the code block and that language is supported by highlight.js, the code is highlighted with that language.md.render(markdown) converts markdown text to HTML. This is the core functionality of markdown-it. The convertDirectory function goes through each markdown file in the given directory, reads the file, renders the markdown to HTML, and writes the HTML back to a file with the same name but with a .html extension.markdown-it was chosen over the default because it has more features and is more extensible than the default marked package used in the project. markdown-it supports a wide range of markdown syntax features, and you can add even more with plugins. You can also customize how the rendering behaves with options and by replacing or wrapping the default rendering rules.Compared to other markdown parsers, markdown-it stands out with its combination of performance, flexibility, and features. It's one of the fastest CommonMark-compliant parsers, and it provides a solid and extensible core for all kinds of markdown processing tasks. The architecture of markdown-it allows you to replace the rendering rules for any token type, which gives you a lot of control over the output.The decision to choose one library over another depends on the specific requirements and constraints of your project. If you want more control over the rendering and you need support for a wide range of markdown syntax, then markdown-it is a good choice. If you need something simpler and smaller, or you have different requirements, then another library might be more suitable.

This is different from using a dynamic site generator like Jekyll, Hugo, or Gatsby.Static site generators like Jekyll create a fully rendered HTML website at build time, usually from markdown files. Jekyll, in particular, is often used with GitHub Pages. However, it uses a templating language called Liquid, which can add complexity for some users.In contrast, the script above uses markdown-it to convert markdown files to HTML one by one. It's more of a "roll your own" approach, where we're manually controlling the conversion process. This can be a simpler and more flexible approach for some projects. For instance, you can modify the script to include extra processing steps, like inserting dynamic content or applying custom formatting.Also, an important point to mention is the use of the .nojekyll file in the script. GitHub Pages uses Jekyll by default to build and serve your site. When GitHub Pages sees the .nojekyll file, it skips the Jekyll build process entirely. This is necessary here because we're bypassing Jekyll and converting markdown to HTML ourselves with markdown-it.So, in this context, we're choosing markdown-it over a dynamic site generator (Jekyll) for the sake of simplicity, control, and flexibility. But again, the best choice depends on the specific needs and constraints of your project.

#!/bin/sh

# Goal: Make "npx junior-web" start web.js
# Plan:
# 1. Modify package.json to add "junior-web" command to the bin object and change the "start" script.
# 2. Add shebang to web.js.
# 3. Make web.js executable.

# Step 1: Modify package.json
jq '.bin += {"junior-web": "src/web.js"} | .scripts.start = "node src/web.js"' package.json > package.json.tmp && mv package.json.tmp package.json

# Step 2: Add shebang to web.js
echo '#!/usr/bin/env node' | cat - src/web.js > temp && mv temp src/web.js

# Step 3: Make web.js executable
chmod +x src/web.js

#!/bin/sh
# Goal: Rename build:docs to build:doc in package.json
# Plan:

Conversations.Prompt: How does markdownIt works? Why did you choose it over the default, and why over others?
Conversations.Answer: markdown-it is a very powerful and flexible markdown parser and renderer for Node.js. It's highly extensible and customizable with plugins, and it supports all markdown syntax features, including some features not found in other markdown parsers.Here's a brief explanation of how markdown-it works in the context of the script provided:markdownIt() initializes a new markdown-it instance with certain options. html: true enables HTML tags in the source, linkify: true autoconverts URL-like text to links, and typographer: true enables some language-neutral replacement and typographic symbols.highlight is a function that gets called whenever markdown-it encounters code blocks in the markdown source. Here it's using highlight.js to highlight the code in the code blocks. If a language is specified with the code block and that language is supported by highlight.js, the code is highlighted with that language.md.render(markdown) converts markdown text to HTML. This is the core functionality of markdown-it. The convertDirectory function goes through each markdown file in the given directory, reads the file, renders the markdown to HTML, and writes the HTML back to a file with the same name but with a .html extension.markdown-it was chosen over the default because it has more features and is more extensible than the default marked package used in the project. markdown-it supports a wide range of markdown syntax features, and you can add even more with plugins. You can also customize how the rendering behaves with options and by replacing or wrapping the default rendering rules.Compared to other markdown parsers, markdown-it stands out with its combination of performance, flexibility, and features. It's one of the fastest CommonMark-compliant parsers, and it provides a solid and extensible core for all kinds of markdown processing tasks. The architecture of markdown-it allows you to replace the rendering rules for any token type, which gives you a lot of control over the output.The decision to choose one library over another depends on the specific requirements and constraints of your project. If you want more control over the rendering and you need support for a wide range of markdown syntax, then markdown-it is a good choice. If you need something simpler and smaller, or you have different requirements, then another library might be more suitable.

They provide clarity about what each script does, which can make navigation and maintenance easier. import * as vscode from 'vscode';
import * as fs from 'fs';
import * as path from 'path';
import * as yaml from 'js-yaml';
import { filterAttentionExcludes } from './filterAttentionExcludes';

export const writeAttention = async () => {
    const workspaceFolders = vscode.workspace.workspaceFolders;
    if (workspaceFolders === undefined) {
        return;
    }
    
    const rootFolder = workspaceFolders[0].uri.fsPath;
    const promptFilePath = path.join(rootFolder, 'prompt.yaml');
    const excludeList = vscode.workspace.getConfiguration('junior').get('attentionExcludeList', []);
    try {
        if (fs.existsSync(promptFilePath)) {
            const currentWindows = vscode.workspace.textDocuments.map(doc => path.relative(rootFolder, doc.fileName));
            const filteredWindows = filterAttentionExcludes(currentWindows, excludeList, rootFolder);
            const promptFile: any = yaml.load(fs.readFileSync(promptFilePath, 'utf8'));
            promptFile.attention = filteredWindows;
            fs.writeFileSync(promptFilePath, yaml.dump(promptFile), 'utf8');
            vscode.window.showInformationMessage('Prompt file updated successfully!');
        } else {
            vscode.window.showErrorMessage('No prompt.yaml file found in the project root!');
        }
    } catch (error) {
        vscode.window.showErrorMessage('Error updating the prompt.yaml file!');
    }
};

import * as glob from 'glob';
import * as path from 'path';
import * as fs from 'fs';

export const filterAttentionExcludes = (windowPaths: string[], excludeList: string[], rootFolder: string) => {
    return windowPaths.filter(windowPath => {
        return !windowPath.endsWith('.git') && windowPath !== 'prompt.yaml' && windowPath !== 'prompt.md' && windowPath !== 'change.sh' && !excludeList.some((pattern) => glob.sync(pattern, { cwd: rootFolder }).includes(windowPath)) && fs.existsSync(path.join(rootFolder, windowPath));
    });
}

# The Junior - Your AI contributor which writes itself.

## Description

The Contributor is an exploratory project aimed at revolutionizing the way programmers interact with the development process. Just like how Linus Torvalds oversees the Linux Kernel development without coding himself, this project allows developers to communicate with the AI and supervise the development process.

By providing specific task details in a prompt descriptor and highlighting the relevant parts of your project, you can delegate code implementation, documentation, testing, and more to your AI Contributor.

## Getting Started

### Installation

To install, clone the repository and run `npm install` in the root directory.

### Usage

There are two ways to use this project: a command-line interface (CLI) and a web interface.

#### Command-line interface (CLI)

To start the CLI, use `npm run cli`. This mode uses the ChatGPT API, and you'll need an API key stored in the `OPENAI_API_KEY` environment variable.

#### Web Interface

Run the application with `npm start` to start a local server on port 3000, where you can generate a prompt and automatically copy it to paste into ChatGPT. The web interface is designed for use with ChatGPT Pro and doesn't require an API key.

### The Prompt Descriptor

A prompt descriptor is a YAML file (`prompt.yaml`) outlining the details necessary for generating a task prompt for the AI model.

Here's an example of a prompt descriptor:

```yaml
task: prompt/task/feature/implement.md
attention:
  - src/interactiveSession/startInteractiveSession.js
  - src/prompt/createPrompt.js
  - src/attention/readAttention.js
  - prompt.yaml
requirements: >
  Write a README.md for this _exploratory_ project!
format: prompt/format/new_file_version.md
```

Each element in the descriptor serves a specific purpose:
- `task`: Describes the task type and scope. For example, `feature/implement`, `bug/fix`, or `refactor/`. You can check out the [prompt/task/feature/implement.md](prompt/task/feature/implement.md) file as an example.
- `attention`: Lists the files and directories most relevant to the task.
- `requirements`: Describes the actual task in a human-readable format.
- `format`: Determines how the output will be formatted.

### Attention Mechanism

The attention mechanism guides the AI model by providing it with a working set. It helps overcome the limited working memory of large language models.

The working set is a subset of the entire project that's currently in focus. It includes both files and directories. For files, the content is directly provided to the AI. For directories, a brief list of files and subdirectories within them is presented.

## Contributing and Support

Contributions are welcome! Remember, we eat our own dog food in this project. This project is designed to write itself. Your main role will be to oversee the work, provide detailed prompts, and review the outcomes.

For support, please create an issue in the GitHub repository.

**Note:** For meaningful results, it's recommended to use the GPT-4 model or a more recent version.

Conversations.Answer: The issue with your code is that you are performing an AJAX request (using fetch) on the client side, which means you are sending the data asynchronously to the server and handling the response in JavaScript. The response.redirect method on the server side, which performs a redirect, only affects the server's response, not the client's browser.To achieve a redirect on the client side, you can modify your client-side code to handle the redirect after receiving a successful response from the server. Here's an example of how you can modify your code to achieve the desired redirect:[CODE_BLOCK_0]In the modified code, after receiving a successful response (response.ok), window.location.href is set to the URL provided by the server in the response. This will trigger a redirect on the client side, and the browser will navigate to the specified URL.

Conversations.Prompt: I see. That clarifies some things. Could you also explain to me why submitting a form using EJS and body-parser works with no issues instead? What's the difference?
Conversations.Answer: When you submit a form using EJS and body-parser, the form submission triggers a traditional synchronous POST request from the client's browser to the server. In this case, the server can respond with a redirect, and the client's browser will automatically follow that redirect and navigate to the specified URL.The key difference between this approach and the previous AJAX approach is the nature of the request and the way the client handles the response. In the AJAX approach, the JavaScript code on the client side sends the request asynchronously and receives the response in JavaScript without triggering a full page reload. This allows for more dynamic and interactive web applications.When you use EJS and body-parser to submit a form, the browser sends a regular form submission request synchronously, causing the browser to navigate to the URL specified in the form's action attribute. This behavior is the default behavior of HTML forms. The server can then respond with a redirect using the response.redirect method, and the browser will automatically follow that redirect, resulting in a page navigation.In summary, the difference lies in how the request is sent and how the response is handled. The AJAX approach allows for asynchronous communication between the client and the server, enabling dynamic updates without page reloads. On the other hand, submitting a form using EJS and body-parser triggers a synchronous request-response cycle that causes the browser to navigate to the redirected URL.

Fix mdns publishing service to stop growing json cache

- `pgrep` could not see the `avahi-publish` processes so it was constantly thinking they had not been started and thus kept adding to the cached JSON.
- Used `avahi-resolve` instead to check if a domain had been published rather than trying to get a list of published domains.
- The downside of using `avahi-resolve` isif it is not already published then it waits a timeout before it returns
- OTOH since this is a background task running on a timer the timeout will only ever create issues when modifying the script and having to wait for timeout while debugging. Hopefully this won't be needed much.
- See https://chat.openai.com/share/27c1d73c-015b-4546-b1fa-7b9f55a6b775 for background.

```
#!/usr/bin/env bash

HOST_IP_ADDRESS="$(hostname -I | awk '{print$1}')"
HOST_PORT="8081"
TRAEFIK_ROUTERS_API_URL="http://${HOST_IP_ADDRESS}:${HOST_PORT}/api/http/routers"
CACHE_FILE="/etc/traefik/traefik-mdns.json"

function is_debug {
  local is_debug="$1"
  if [ "debug" == "${is_debug}" ] ; then
    echo 1
    return
  fi
  echo 0
}

DEBUG="$(is_debug "$1")"

function debug_msg {
  local msg="$1"
  if [ $DEBUG -eq 1 ] ; then
    printf "\n%s" "${msg}"
  fi
}

function publish_domain {
  local host_ip="$1"
  local domain="$2"

  /usr/bin/avahi-publish -a "${domain}" -R "${host_ip}" &
}

function read_cached_json {
  local cached_json=""

  if [ -f "${CACHE_FILE}" ] ; then
    cached_json="$(cat "${CACHE_FILE}")"
  fi

  if [ "" != "${cached_json}" ] ; then
    echo "${cached_json}"
  else
    echo '{"domains":[]}' | sudo tee "${CACHE_FILE}"
    return
  fi
}

function write_cached_json {
  local cached_json="$1"
  printf "%s" "${cached_json}" | sudo tee "${CACHE_FILE}" >/dev/null
}

function extract_cached_domains {
  local cached_json="$1"
  if [ "${cached_json}" == "" ] ; then
    cached_json="$(read_cached_json)"
  fi
  jq -r '.domains[]|.name' <<< "${cached_json}" \
    | sort \
    | tr "\n" ' '
}

# Dedups a space-separated list of domains
function dedup_domains {
  local domains="$1"
  tr ' ' "\n" <<< "${domains}" \
    | sort \
    | uniq \
    | tr "\n" ' '
}

function cache_has_domain {
  local domain="$1"
  local cached_domains="$2"
  local query

  query="$(printf '.domains[]|select(.name=="%s")' "${domain}")"
  result="$(jq -r "${query}" <<< "${cached_domains}")"
  test "" != "${result}"
}

function add_domain {
  local domain="$1"
  local cached_domains="$2"
  local query

  query="$(printf '.domains += [{"name":"%s", "last_seen": "%s"}]' "${domain}" "$(current_iso8601_datetime)")"
  jq "${query}" <<< "${cached_domains}"
}

function update_domain {
  local domain="$1"
  local cached_domains="$2"
  local query

  query="$(printf '.domains |= map(if .name == "%s" then .last_seen = "%s" else . end)' "${domain}" "$(current_iso8601_datetime)")"
  jq "${query}" <<< "${cached_domains}"
}

function current_iso8601_datetime {
  # Example: 2023-06-29T05:52:18Z where Z means UTC
  date -u +"%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ"
}

function retrieve_routers_json {
  curl --silent "${TRAEFIK_ROUTERS_API_URL}"
}

function discover_published_domains {
  pgrep -a avahi-publish | awk '{print $4}' | tr "\n" ' '
}

function kill_published {
  pgrep avahi-publish | xargs kill -9
}

#
function extract_retrieved_domains {
  local routers_json="$1"

  jq -e '.[] | select(.rule|contains("Host(`"))|.rule' <<< "${routers_json}" \
      | tr '`' ' ' \
      | awk '{print$2}' \
      | sort \
      | uniq \
      | tr "\n" ' '
}

# Timing out domains last seen more than 24 hours ago.
function timeout_domains {
  local timeout_hours="$1"
  local cached_json="$2"
  local map
  local query
  local yesterday_seconds

  yesterday_seconds="$(( $(date +%s) - 60*60*timeout_hours ))"
  map="$(printf 'map(select((.last_seen | strptime("%s") | mktime)' "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ")"
  query="$(printf '.domains |= %s > %d))' "${map}" "${yesterday_seconds}")"
  jq "${query}" <<< "${cached_json}"
}

function main() {
  local space=' '
  local updated=0
  local routers_json
  local published_domains
  local cached_json
  local cached_domains
  local retrieved_domains
  local potential_domains
  local domain

  debug_msg "Read the cache file to find any domains that were previously there."
  cached_json="$(read_cached_json)"

  debug_msg "Time out domains last seen more than 24 hours ago."
  cached_json="$(timeout_domains 24 "${cached_json}")"

  debug_msg "Extract cached domains from cached json that was read from the cache file."
  cached_domains=$(extract_cached_domains "${cached_json}")

  debug_msg "Send an HTTP GET request to retrieve the routers JSON from Traefik API."
  routers_json="$(retrieve_routers_json)"
  if [ "${routers_json}" == "" ] ; then
    printf 'Warning: Unable to reach %s' "${TRAEFIK_ROUTERS_API_URL}" >&2
  fi

  debug_msg "Extract just the .local domains retrieved in Traefik into a space-separated string."
  retrieved_domains="$(extract_retrieved_domains "${routers_json}")"

  debug_msg "Combine Traefik-defined domains an previously cached domains into potential domains."
  potential_domains="${cached_domains} ${retrieved_domains}"

  debug_msg "Deduplicate domains after combining Traefik-defined and previously cached domains."
  potential_domains="$(dedup_domains "${potential_domains}")"

  debug_msg "Use pgrep to discover the avahi-published .local domains from list of processes."
  published_domains="$(discover_published_domains)"

  debug_msg "Loop through the domains retrieved from Traefik to see if they have been published."
  for domain in $potential_domains; do
    debug_msg "Attempt to match a .local domain retrieved from Trafik to the list of domains currently published."
    debug_msg "$(printf 'Checking if %s is published_domains...' "${domain}")"
    if [[ "${space}${published_domains}${space}" =~ ${space}${domain}${space} ]] ; then
      [ $DEBUG -eq 1 ] && printf "already published"
      debug_msg "$(printf 'Updating .last_seen %s in cache file %s.' "${domain}", "${CACHE_FILE}")"
      debug_msg 'Since the domain is already published update JSON with last seen time.'
      if cache_has_domain "${domain}" "${cached_json}" ; then
        cached_json="$(update_domain "${domain}" "${cached_json}")"
      else
        cached_json="$(add_domain "${domain}" "${cached_json}")"
      fi
      debug_msg 'Now look at the next domain.'
      continue
    fi
    printf "Publishing %s\n" "${domain}"
    if ! publish_domain "${HOST_IP_ADDRESS}" "${domain}"; then
      printf 'Error: Unable to publish %s' "${domain}" >&2
    fi
    debug_msg "$(printf 'Adding %s to cache file %s.' "${domain}" "${CACHE_FILE}")"
    cached_json="$(add_domain "${domain}" "${cached_json}")"
    updated=1
    debug_msg "Write updated JSON to CACHE_FILE"
  done
  if [ "" != "${retrieved_domains}" ]; then
    debug_msg "Writing cache."
    write_cached_json "${cached_json}"
  fi
  if [ $DEBUG -eq 1 ]; then
    printf "\n"
  fi
  if [ $updated -eq 1 ]; then
    printf "\n"
  fi
}

main
```

Conversations.Answer: From the information provided, it's possible that the issue might be related to the environment in which the systemd service is running. systemd services don't have the same environment variables as an interactive shell, and your script may depend on some of these variables.Here are some steps that you can take to debug and potentially resolve the issue:Verify that the necessary commands are accessible: The systemd service may not have the same PATH as your user's interactive shell. You could specify the absolute paths for all the commands in your bash script, or set the PATH in your systemd service file.Add error logging to your script: Modify your bash script to log errors to a file. This might provide more insight into what's going wrong when the script is run as a systemd service. You can add something like the following at the beginning of your script:[CODE_BLOCK_0]This will redirect all error messages to /path/to/your/logfile.log.Check environment differences: You can compare the environment variables available in the systemd service and in the interactive shell. You could modify your script to dump its environment to a file using env > /tmp/env.dump and then compare this with the environment of your interactive shell.Ensure the correct user and permissions: If your script needs to run as a specific user or requires special permissions, you should specify this in your service file using the User= and Group= directives under [Service]. Additionally, make sure the script file has the necessary executable permissions.Add Restart=on-failure in your service file: This will tell systemd to restart the service if it fails. Sometimes services fail and stop completely. This directive ensures that your service is restarted when it fails:[CODE_BLOCK_1]Try with Type=simple instead of Type=oneshot: In your systemd service file, you have specified Type=oneshot, which means that systemd considers the service started once the process exits. This can cause problems with services that spawn child processes and exit (which appears to be what your script does). You could try changing this to Type=simple.[CODE_BLOCK_2]After making these modifications, remember to reload the systemd daemon using sudo systemctl daemon-reload and then try to start your service again with sudo systemctl start traefik-mdns.service.Inspect the logs with sudo systemctl status traefik-mdns.service and journalctl -u traefik-mdns.service to see if there are any noticeable changes or errors.

Conversations.Prompt: What is the difference between service types `simple` and  `forking`?
Conversations.Answer: The Type directive in a systemd service file specifies the process behavior that systemd should expect when the service is started. The values simple and forking have different implications:Type=simple (default): With this setting, systemd expects that the process launched by ExecStart is the main process of the service. This is the default value if no Type is specified. If this process exits, systemd considers the service to be stopped.Type=forking: In this case, systemd expects that the process launched by ExecStart will fork, and that the parent process will exit when startup is complete and the service is running. The remaining child process will continue to run as the main process of the service. This is useful for services that traditionally were written to follow the Unix fork/exec model (i.e., the process "daemonizes" itself by forking a child process and then having the parent process immediately exit).For Type=forking, it's often used with the PIDFile directive, which points to the PID file of the service. This is necessary for systemd to keep track of the main (child) process.In short, use Type=simple for services that can run in the foreground and don't need to fork themselves. If your service needs to follow the traditional Unix daemon style (i.e., it needs to fork a child and have the parent process exit), use Type=forking. But as software has evolved, it's often considered better to let the process manager (in this case, systemd) handle the backgrounding of services, so Type=simple is generally preferred unless the service explicitly needs the forking behavior.

ChatgptSharing.Title: Rename Go files to snake case

Conversations.Prompt: My codebase has a lot of old Go code which uses camel case file names like `tlsConfigHelper.go`. I'd like for all of these files to be renamed to use snake case like `tls_config_helper.go`. Can you write a bash script which will do this?
Conversations.Answer: Certainly! Here's a bash script that can help you rename the Go files from camel case to snake case:[CODE_BLOCK_0]Make sure to replace /path/to/your/codebase with the actual path to your codebase's root folder.Here's how the script works:It changes the current directory to your codebase root folder.It uses the find command to search for all Go files with camel case names.The resulting file paths are filtered using grep to exclude files that don't have a lowercase followed by an uppercase letter in their paths.For each file, it extracts the directory and base name.It converts the camel case base name to snake case using sed and tr.It constructs the new file name by appending the snake case base name to the original directory path.It renames the file using the mv command.Finally, it prints a message indicating the file has been renamed.Please be cautious when running scripts that modify your codebase, and consider making a backup or using version control before executing this script.

ListOfCode.Content:
#!/bin/bash

# Change directory to your codebase root folder
cd /path/to/your/codebase

# Find all Go files with camel case names
files=$(find . -type f -name "*.go" | grep -P '.*\/[a-z]+[A-Z]+.*')

# Loop through each file and rename it
for file in $files; do
  # Get the file's directory and base name
  dir=$(dirname "$file")
  base=$(basename "$file")

  # Convert camel case to snake case
  snake_case=$(echo "$base" | sed -E 's/([^A-Z])([A-Z])/\1_\2/g' | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]')

  # Construct the new file name
  new_name="$dir/$(dirname "$base")_$snake_case"

  # Rename the file
  mv "$file" "$new_name"

  echo "Renamed $file to $new_name"
done

#!/usr/bin/env python3

import os
import re
import subprocess

def camel_to_snake(name):
    """Converts a camel case string to snake case."""
    result = ""
    for i, char in enumerate(name):
        if char.isupper() and (i == 0 or (i > 0 and name[i-1].islower())):
            result += char.lower()
        elif char.isupper() and i > 0:
            result += "_" + char.lower()
        else:
            result += char.lower()
    return result

def git_mv(old_path, new_path):
    """Renames a file using 'git mv'."""
    subprocess.run(['git', 'mv', old_path, new_path])

def update_generate_statements(file_path):
    """Updates the go:generate statements in a Go source code file."""
    with open(file_path, 'r+') as file:
        content = file.read()

        # Match go:generate statements with mockgen command
        pattern = r'//go:generate\s+mockgen\s+.*-destination\s+(\S+)\s*'
        matches = re.findall(pattern, content)

        if matches:
            for match in matches:
                old_path = match
                new_path = camel_to_snake(match)
                updated_content = content.replace(old_path, new_path)
                file.seek(0)
                file.write(updated_content)
                file.truncate()

def main():
    # Change directory to your codebase root folder
    os.chdir(os.path.join(os.environ['HOME'], 'src/temporalio/temporal'))

    # Loop through each file in the directory and its subdirectories
    for root, dirs, files in os.walk('.'):
        for file in files:
            if file.endswith('.go'):
                old_path = os.path.join(root, file)
                new_name = camel_to_snake(file[:-3]) + '.go'
                new_path = os.path.join(root, new_name)

                # Rename the file using 'git mv'
                git_mv(old_path, new_path)
                print(f"Renamed {old_path} to {new_path}")

                # Update go:generate statements in the file
                update_generate_statements(new_path)
                print(f"Updated go:generate statements in {new_path}")

if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

#!/usr/bin/env python3

import os
import re
import subprocess

def camel_to_snake(name):
    """Converts a camel case string to snake case."""
    name = name.replace("nDC", "ndc")

    for char in name:
        if char.isupper() and prev_char.islower():
            result += "_" + char.lower()
        else:
            result += char.lower()
        prev_char = char
    return result

def git_mv(old_path, new_path):
    """Renames a file using 'git mv'."""
    subprocess.run(['git', 'mv', old_path, new_path])

def rename_file(old_path):
    """Renames a file using 'git mv' and updates go:generate statements."""
    base_name = os.path.basename(old_path)
    new_name = None

    if base_name.endswith("Test.go"):
        prefix = base_name[:-len("Test.go")]
        new_name = "test_" + camel_to_snake(prefix) + ".go"
    else:
        new_name = camel_to_snake(base_name)

    new_path = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(old_path), new_name)
    git_mv(old_path, new_path)
    print(f"Renamed {old_path} to {new_path}")

    update_generate_statements(new_path)
    print(f"Updated go:generate statements in {new_path}")

def update_generate_statements(file_path):
    """Updates the go:generate statements in a Go source code file."""
    with open(file_path, 'r+') as file:
        content = file.read()

        # Match go:generate statements with mockgen command
        pattern = r'//go:generate\s+mockgen\s+.*-destination\s+(\S+)\s*'
        matches = re.findall(pattern, content)

        if matches:
            for match in matches:
                old_path = match
                new_path = camel_to_snake(match)
                updated_content = content.replace(old_path, new_path)
                file.seek(0)
                file.write(updated_content)
                file.truncate()

def main():
    # Change directory to your codebase root folder
    os.chdir(os.path.join(os.environ['HOME'], 'src/temporalio/temporal'))

    # Loop through each file in the directory and its subdirectories
    for root, dirs, files in os.walk('.'):
        for file in files:
            if file.endswith('.go'):
                file_path = os.path.join(root, file)
                rename_file(file_path)

Set up npm test in a github action. (#9)

https://chat.openai.com/share/c18aff35-93b2-4274-83c3-dc005b4812a2

I'm trying to set up the github action for running npm test but it
complains that there's no package-lock.json

ChatGPT
GitHub Actions is a tool that enables you to automate, customize, and
execute your software development workflows right in your GitHub
repository.

You're seeing an error message because your repository doesn't have a
package-lock.json file. The package-lock.json file is automatically
generated when npm install is run and it describes the exact tree that
was generated such that subsequent installs are able to generate
identical trees, regardless of intermediate dependency updates.

Here are a few ways to resolve this:

Add a package-lock.json file:
Run npm install in your project's root directory locally. This will
create a package-lock.json file if there isn't one already.
Commit and push the package-lock.json file to your GitHub repository.
Use npm ci instead of npm install:
If you're using npm install in your GitHub Actions workflow, you may
want to switch to npm ci. npm ci is a more reliable and faster
alternative for continuous integration environments. However, it
requires a package-lock.json or npm-shrinkwrap.json file to be present.
Here's a basic example of a GitHub Actions workflow file for running npm
test:

```yaml
name: Node.js CI

on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    strategy:
      matrix:
        node-version: [14.x]

    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v2
    - name: Use Node.js ${{ matrix.node-version }}
      uses: actions/setup-node@v2
      with:
        node-version: ${{ matrix.node-version }}
    - run: npm ci
    - run: npm test
```

Remember that you still need to commit and push your package-lock.json
or npm-shrinkwrap.json file to your GitHub repository to use npm ci.

Disable the package-lock.json check:
If you don't want to use a package-lock.json file, you can disable the
check in your .npmrc file by adding the following line:

```npm
package-lock=false
```

Please note that by doing this, you lose the benefits of having a
package-lock.json file. Also, make sure to update your GitHub Actions
workflow to use npm install instead of npm ci, because npm ci requires a
package-lock.json or npm-shrinkwrap.json file to work.

Added package-lock.json to the repo.

```
Run npm ci
npm ERR! Cannot read property 'text-encoding' of undefined

npm ERR! A complete log of this run can be found in:
npm ERR!     /home/runner/.npm/_logs/2023-07-04T20_22_56_587Z-debug.log
Error: Process completed with exit code 1.
```

ChatGPT
This error is indicating that there is an issue in your
package-lock.json file. The error you're seeing is typically caused by a
mismatch between the versions of npm that were used to create the
package-lock.json file and the version that you are currently using. The
npm ci command requires an accurate package-lock.json to work, otherwise
it can produce errors.

Here are some steps you can take to fix this:

Update npm: If your npm is not up to date, some inconsistencies can
occur. Make sure you're using the same version locally as in your
workflow. You can update npm using the command npm install -g npm.

Regenerate package-lock.json: If updating npm didn't solve the problem,
try deleting package-lock.json and node_modules then run npm install to
generate a new package-lock.json. Make sure to push the new
package-lock.json to your repository.

```shell
rm -rf node_modules package-lock.json
npm install
git add package-lock.json
git commit -m "Updated package-lock.json"
git push
```

Specify the Node.js and npm version in the workflow: You can specify the
Node.js and npm version in your workflow to ensure the same versions are
used in your local and CI environment.

```yaml
steps:
- uses: actions/checkout@v2
- name: Use Node.js 14.x
  uses: actions/setup-node@v2
  with:
    node-version: 14.x
- name: Install npm
  run: npm install -g npm@6
- run: npm ci
- run: npm test

[Eval] Viewport to grid size (#1083)

# Thank you for contributing an eval! ♥️

🚨 Please make sure your PR follows these guidelines, __failure to follow
the guidelines below will result in the PR being closed automatically__.
Note that even if the criteria are met, that does not guarantee the PR
will be merged nor GPT-4 access granted. 🚨

__PLEASE READ THIS__:

In order for a PR to be merged, it must fail on GPT-4. We are aware that
right now, users do not have access, so you will not be able to tell if
the eval fails or not. Please run your eval with GPT-3.5-Turbo, but keep
in mind as we run the eval, if GPT-4 gets higher than 90% on the eval,
we will likely reject since GPT-4 is already capable of completing the
task.

We plan to roll out a way for users submitting evals to see the eval
performance on GPT-4 soon. Stay tuned! Until then, you will not be able
to see the eval performance on GPT-4. **Starting April 10, the minimum
eval count is 15 samples, we hope this makes it easier to create and
contribute evals.**

Also, pelase note that we're using **Git LFS** for storing the JSON
files, so please make sure that you move the JSON file to Git LFS before
submitting a PR. Details on how to use Git LFS are available
[here](https://git-lfs.com).

## Eval details 📑
### Eval name
viewport_to_grid_size

### Eval description
Evaluates a models ability to determine the size of an obscured grid
using information only from initial constraints and a visible viewport.

### What makes this a useful eval?

Requires the model to go beyond simple instruction following to solve a
task that requires pattern recognition and interpretation.


<details>
  <summary>"GPT4 Pattern Recognition"</summary>


> The AI could benefit from better pattern recognition in problems like
this, to understand how the relationship between parts of a system (like
a viewport and a larger grid) can reveal information about the whole
system.
https://chat.openai.com/share/4aeb8ed6-6dff-4f26-a946-aefe8c2fa511


I provided the prompt (submitted in this eval) to ChatGPT and tried to
get it to reword the prompt by telling it that I didn't understand it.

<details>
  <summary>(original) prompt for reference</summary>


`Given a viewport into a larger grid, calculate the total number of
cells in the grid. The grid consists of cells, each labeled with an
index. The labeling starts at 1 in the first cell located in the top
left corner of the grid and increments by 1 with each step. The final
cell in the bottom right corner of the grid is the size of the grid. The
viewport shows only a small portion of the (square) grid. Provide the
answer directly, or the mathematical representation e.g (rows * cols)`
</details>

GPT-4 proceeded to misinterpret the task (which I expected), but when I
challenged it's assumptions with the original facts provided it realized
that my original instructions were sufficient and the prompt didn't
require any changing.
> The original instructions you provided were quite clear in retrospect.
The misunderstanding was on my part for not correctly identifying the
pattern from the viewport. The instructions were providing all necessary
information for someone to identify the grid size by observing the
numerical pattern in the viewport.


</details>

## Criteria for a good eval ✅

Below are some of the criteria we look for in a good eval. In general,
we are seeking cases where the model does not do a good job despite
being capable of generating a good response (note that there are some
things large language models cannot do, so those would not make good
evals).

Your eval should be:

- [x] Thematically consistent: The eval should be thematically
consistent. We'd like to see a number of prompts all demonstrating some
particular failure mode. For example, we can create an eval on cases
where the model fails to reason about the physical world.
- [x] Contains failures where a human can do the task, but either GPT-4
or GPT-3.5-Turbo could not.
- [x] Includes good signal around what is the right behavior. This means
either a correct answer for `Basic` evals or the `Fact` Model-graded
eval, or an exhaustive rubric for evaluating answers for the `Criteria`
Model-graded eval.
- [x] **Include at least 15 high quality examples.**

If there is anything else that makes your eval worth including, please
document it below.

### Unique eval value

## Eval structure 🏗️

Your eval should
- [x] Check that your data is in `evals/registry/data/{name}`
- [x] Check that your yaml is registered at
`evals/registry/evals/{name}.yaml`
- [x] Ensure you have the right to use the data you submit via this eval

(For now, we will only be approving evals that use one of the existing
eval classes. You may still write custom eval classes for your own
cases, and we may consider merging them in the future.)

## Final checklist 👀

### Submission agreement

By contributing to Evals, you are agreeing to make your evaluation logic
and data under the same MIT license as this repository. You must have
adequate rights to upload any data used in an Eval. OpenAI reserves the
right to use this data in future service improvements to our product.
Contributions to OpenAI Evals will be subject to our usual Usage
Policies (https://platform.openai.com/docs/usage-policies).

- [x] I agree that my submission will be made available under an MIT
license and complies with OpenAI's usage policies.

### Email address validation

If your submission is accepted, we will be granting GPT-4 access to a
limited number of contributors. Access will be given to the email
address associated with the merged pull request.

- [x] I acknowledge that GPT-4 access will only be granted, if
applicable, to the email address used for my merged pull request.

### Limited availability acknowledgement

We know that you might be excited to contribute to OpenAI's mission,
help improve our models, and gain access to GPT-4. However, due to the
requirements mentioned above and high volume of submissions, we will not
be able to accept all submissions and thus not grant everyone who opens
a PR GPT-4 access. We know this is disappointing, but we hope to set the
right expectation before you open this PR.

- [x] I understand that opening a PR, even if it meets the requirements
above, does not guarantee the PR will be merged nor GPT-4 access
granted.

### Submit eval

- [x] I have filled out all required fields of this form
- [x] I have used **Git LFS** for the Eval JSON data
- [ ] (Ignore if not submitting code) I have run `pip install
pre-commit; pre-commit install` and have verified that `black`, `isort`,
and `autoflake` are running when I commit and push

Failure to fill out all required fields will result in the PR being
closed.

[Eval] Viewport to grid size (#1083)

# Thank you for contributing an eval! ♥️

🚨 Please make sure your PR follows these guidelines, __failure to follow
the guidelines below will result in the PR being closed automatically__.
Note that even if the criteria are met, that does not guarantee the PR
will be merged nor GPT-4 access granted. 🚨

__PLEASE READ THIS__:

In order for a PR to be merged, it must fail on GPT-4. We are aware that
right now, users do not have access, so you will not be able to tell if
the eval fails or not. Please run your eval with GPT-3.5-Turbo, but keep
in mind as we run the eval, if GPT-4 gets higher than 90% on the eval,
we will likely reject since GPT-4 is already capable of completing the
task.

We plan to roll out a way for users submitting evals to see the eval
performance on GPT-4 soon. Stay tuned! Until then, you will not be able
to see the eval performance on GPT-4. **Starting April 10, the minimum
eval count is 15 samples, we hope this makes it easier to create and
contribute evals.**

Also, pelase note that we're using **Git LFS** for storing the JSON
files, so please make sure that you move the JSON file to Git LFS before
submitting a PR. Details on how to use Git LFS are available
[here](https://git-lfs.com).

## Eval details 📑
### Eval name
viewport_to_grid_size

### Eval description
Evaluates a models ability to determine the size of an obscured grid
using information only from initial constraints and a visible viewport.

### What makes this a useful eval?

Requires the model to go beyond simple instruction following to solve a
task that requires pattern recognition and interpretation.


<details>
  <summary>"GPT4 Pattern Recognition"</summary>


> The AI could benefit from better pattern recognition in problems like
this, to understand how the relationship between parts of a system (like
a viewport and a larger grid) can reveal information about the whole
system.
https://chat.openai.com/share/4aeb8ed6-6dff-4f26-a946-aefe8c2fa511


I provided the prompt (submitted in this eval) to ChatGPT and tried to
get it to reword the prompt by telling it that I didn't understand it.

<details>
  <summary>(original) prompt for reference</summary>


`Given a viewport into a larger grid, calculate the total number of
cells in the grid. The grid consists of cells, each labeled with an
index. The labeling starts at 1 in the first cell located in the top
left corner of the grid and increments by 1 with each step. The final
cell in the bottom right corner of the grid is the size of the grid. The
viewport shows only a small portion of the (square) grid. Provide the
answer directly, or the mathematical representation e.g (rows * cols)`
</details>

GPT-4 proceeded to misinterpret the task (which I expected), but when I
challenged it's assumptions with the original facts provided it realized
that my original instructions were sufficient and the prompt didn't
require any changing.
> The original instructions you provided were quite clear in retrospect.
The misunderstanding was on my part for not correctly identifying the
pattern from the viewport. The instructions were providing all necessary
information for someone to identify the grid size by observing the
numerical pattern in the viewport.


</details>

## Criteria for a good eval ✅

Below are some of the criteria we look for in a good eval. In general,
we are seeking cases where the model does not do a good job despite
being capable of generating a good response (note that there are some
things large language models cannot do, so those would not make good
evals).

Your eval should be:

- [x] Thematically consistent: The eval should be thematically
consistent. We'd like to see a number of prompts all demonstrating some
particular failure mode. For example, we can create an eval on cases
where the model fails to reason about the physical world.
- [x] Contains failures where a human can do the task, but either GPT-4
or GPT-3.5-Turbo could not.
- [x] Includes good signal around what is the right behavior. This means
either a correct answer for `Basic` evals or the `Fact` Model-graded
eval, or an exhaustive rubric for evaluating answers for the `Criteria`
Model-graded eval.
- [x] **Include at least 15 high quality examples.**

If there is anything else that makes your eval worth including, please
document it below.

### Unique eval value

## Eval structure 🏗️

Your eval should
- [x] Check that your data is in `evals/registry/data/{name}`
- [x] Check that your yaml is registered at
`evals/registry/evals/{name}.yaml`
- [x] Ensure you have the right to use the data you submit via this eval

(For now, we will only be approving evals that use one of the existing
eval classes. You may still write custom eval classes for your own
cases, and we may consider merging them in the future.)

## Final checklist 👀

### Submission agreement

By contributing to Evals, you are agreeing to make your evaluation logic
and data under the same MIT license as this repository. You must have
adequate rights to upload any data used in an Eval. OpenAI reserves the
right to use this data in future service improvements to our product.
Contributions to OpenAI Evals will be subject to our usual Usage
Policies (https://platform.openai.com/docs/usage-policies).

- [x] I agree that my submission will be made available under an MIT
license and complies with OpenAI's usage policies.

### Email address validation

If your submission is accepted, we will be granting GPT-4 access to a
limited number of contributors. Access will be given to the email
address associated with the merged pull request.

- [x] I acknowledge that GPT-4 access will only be granted, if
applicable, to the email address used for my merged pull request.

### Limited availability acknowledgement

We know that you might be excited to contribute to OpenAI's mission,
help improve our models, and gain access to GPT-4. However, due to the
requirements mentioned above and high volume of submissions, we will not
be able to accept all submissions and thus not grant everyone who opens
a PR GPT-4 access. We know this is disappointing, but we hope to set the
right expectation before you open this PR.

- [x] I understand that opening a PR, even if it meets the requirements
above, does not guarantee the PR will be merged nor GPT-4 access
granted.

### Submit eval
